label: Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS

corePack.why: Threat logs are the reason the firewall exists as a security control.
corePack.whyNow: Critical/high signatures are the SOC queue, not a weekly report.
corePack.metric: Threat log count by severity and signature

corePack.why: HA failover and HA1 loss leave the pair without a spare.
corePack.whyNow: The second failure after an unnoticed failover is an outage.
corePack.metric: HA moved-to-active and HA1 heartbeat-loss events

corePack.why: If logs never reach Splunk, every other PAN-OS use case is dark.
corePack.whyNow: Log-forwarding gaps are silent until the next incident review.

corePack.why: Untrusted issuers and expiring decryption certs break inspection and VPNs.
corePack.whyNow: Certificate faults show up as user-visible SSL errors first.
corePack.metric: Certificate inspection and untrusted issuer alerts

corePack.why: Panorama push failures mean the running policy is not the intended policy.
corePack.whyNow: Config drift on the dataplane is a change-control failure in production.

corePack.why: GlobalProtect portal/gateway health is remote-access availability.
corePack.whyNow: VPN down is a workforce outage.

corePack.why: User-ID mapping failures make allow/deny decisions anonymous.
corePack.whyNow: Policy that keys on user/group silently degrades to IP-only.

valueHypothesis: PAN-OS monitoring should start with threat logs, HA health, log forwarding, certificates, and config-push failures. VMware or Fortinet titles that merely mention Palo Alto must not enter this pack.
rationale: Palo Alto operations and HA guides treat threat logging, HA pair health, log forwarding, certificates, and Panorama policy push as the controls that keep the NGFW both effective and available.
